props.title: Man Hunt
props.initialSlug: Nazi target pursues hunter through wartime Europe

sections.content: Fritz Lang's Man Hunt (1941) represents a pivotal moment in Hollywood's anti-Nazi filmmaking, arriving months before Pearl Harbor when America was still officially neutral. The film's opening sequence - where Walter Pidgeon's Captain Thorndike has Hitler in his rifle sights - remains one of cinema's most tensely crafted scenes. Lang, who fled Nazi Germany in 1933, brings his expressionist mastery to this chase thriller, creating shadowy urban landscapes that would influence film noir. The movie shares DNA with other wartime manhunt classics like Foreign Correspondent (1940) and 49th Parallel (1941), but Lang's personal experience with fascism gives it extra bite.

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond its immediate wartime context. Its DNA can be found in later political thrillers like The Day of the Jackal (1973) and Three Days of the Condor (1975). Lang's innovative use of subjective camera angles and claustrophobic framing would become hallmarks of the chase film genre. The cat-and-mouse game between Thorndike and Quive-Smith (George Sanders) established a template for sophisticated hunter-hunted dynamics that echoes through films like North by Northwest (1959).

The film's London sequences showcase Lang's masterful adaptation of German expressionist techniques to Hollywood production values. The fog-shrouded docks and underground tunnels create a gothic atmosphere that prefigures his later noir works like Scarlet Street (1945). Joan Bennett's performance as Jerry, while conforming to some period conventions, brings unexpected depth to what could have been a standard "love interest" role. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of the Chase Thriller

movies.title: Cloak and Dagger
movies.slug: Fritz Lang directs Gary Cooper as a physicist recruited for wartime espionage

sections.content: Man Hunt helped establish crucial elements of the modern chase thriller, particularly in its psychological complexity. Unlike simpler propagandistic films of the era, Lang explores the moral ambiguity of Thorndike's mission and the toll of being hunted. This psychological depth influenced later manhunt films like The Fugitive (1993) and Enemy of the State (1998), where the pursuit becomes as much internal as external.
